## A gate keyed on a NAMED object refuses to build when that object does not exist

**Applies when** an access rule refers to something by name — a role, group, scope, tag, address
list or branch pattern — and the system that enforces it resolves that name only when it evaluates
the rule. Identity-provider flow conditions, policy-engine rules, firewall object groups and
forge branch protections all work this way.

**The rule:** the step that creates or binds the gate checks that every named object exists, and
refuses **before writing anything** when one does not. A test runs that step with a name that does
not exist and expects the refusal; that is the gate's negative control.

**Why:** an unresolved name is not an error at evaluation time. The evaluator falls back to a
default — "nobody matches" or "everybody matches", depending on the product and on whether the
condition is negated — and the build step reports success either way. So a deny-unless-member gate
either admits everyone or locks everyone out, and nothing says which until someone signs in.

**Scope, and its mirrors:**
- **Existence, not membership.** An object that exists and is empty, such as a group created now and
  filled later, is a valid gate. The check is that the name resolves, not that it holds anyone.
- **An object created later by another step** puts an order on the deploy: create the object first,
  or leave the gate unbound until it exists. Never bind first and hope.
- **Build time is not run time.** A rename or delete after the bind breaks the gate the same way, and
  the build check cannot see it. Pair the build check with a periodic report that reads each bound
  gate and resolves its names again.
